analysis.one_liner: Blocks any new federal regulation from taking effect until Congress passes it into law.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee the day it was introduced, received no committee action or floor vote, and died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change how federal rules are made. Today, expert agencies write and issue most federal regulations — clean-air limits, workplace safety rules, food standards — under authority Congress has already granted by law. Under this bill, no regulation could take effect until both the House and Senate passed a bill containing the regulation's exact text and the President signed it. The stated goal was to stop Congress from delegating lawmaking to unelected officials. In practice, it would have let any regulation die simply because Congress chose to do nothing.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses and industries regulated by federal agencies would gain the most: a new clean-air limit, worker-protection rule, or financial rule could be stopped without a single vote — Congress would only need to do nothing. Members of Congress would also gain a form of quiet veto power over every federal rule, taking credit for blocking unpopular regulations without ever having to vote against them on the record.

how_it_helps.text: No regulation could take effect before the enactment of a bill consisting solely of the regulation's text, so every rule would need a majority in the House, a majority in the Senate, and the President's signature.
The bill would give regulation bills an expedited path: no committee referral, debate capped at one hour, no amendments allowed, and a guaranteed vote within 60 days of introduction.
The bill's stated purpose was to end the practice of Congress delegating lawmaking to unelected executive-branch officials and to make elected officials take responsibility for federal rules.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people would bear the cost through weaker and slower federal protections. Rules on air and water pollution, workplace safety, food and drug standards, and consumer finance would each need an act of Congress — a process Congress routinely fails to complete — so protections would stall, lapse, or never arrive.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone relying on federal safety rules

drawbacks.text: Every significant regulation would have to be affirmatively passed by both chambers and signed by the President before taking effect, meaning hundreds of rules each year would enter a legislative process designed to move slowly; any rule Congress failed to act on would simply never exist.

Once a regulation was enacted under the bill, it would no longer count as agency action subject to judicial review under the Administrative Procedure Act, removing a standard avenue for courts to examine the rule.

The bill does carve out some material: rules of particular applicability and interpretive rules, policy statements, and internal agency procedure rules are excluded, so not every agency action would need legislation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The idea behind the bill — that elected officials should answer for the rules that carry the force of law — is a serious constitutional argument, and the expedited procedures show an effort to make congressional votes workable. But the design has a built-in asymmetry: Congress defeats a regulation simply by doing nothing, while saving one requires coordinating two chambers and the President for every rule. That structure would shift the system from rulemaking by accountable experts toward rulemaking by congressional inaction, and the practical effect would be far fewer and weaker federal protections for the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee on the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Sam Brownback introduced the bill on July 12, 1999, joined as original cosponsors by Senators Kyl, Hagel, Allard, Enzi, Sessions, Helms, and Inhofe.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Governmental Affairs the same day, and no further action appears in its history.
It never received a committee or floor vote and died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the existing system of agency rulemaking stayed in place. The people better off are ordinary Americans who rely on federal regulations — clean air and water rules, workplace and consumer protections — that would have become far harder to put in place.

for.name: Sam Brownback
for.role: U.S. Senator from Kansas; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and got it referred to the Governmental Affairs Committee.

for.name: 8 of 55 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (Kyl, Hagel, Allard, Enzi, Sessions, Helms, and Inhofe joined as original cosponsors).

against.name: Senate Committee on Governmental Affairs
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after its referral; it never reached the floor.

against.name: Fred Thompson
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Governmental Affairs
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup, leaving it to die in committee.

sides.party_line_note: Every senator behind the bill — the sponsor and all eight cosponsors — was a Republican, no Democrat signed on, and no roll call was ever taken because the bill never left committee.

industries.note: Under the bill, any new regulation — environmental, safety, financial — could be killed without a vote, since Congress only had to do nothing for a rule to fail. The burden would shift to Congress to affirmatively pass each protection, which it routinely fails to do.
Members would gain an unrecorded veto over every federal rule: inaction kills a regulation, letting opponents block protections without ever casting a visible vote against them.
